title: OSHA Noise Exposure Dose Calculation
problem: Audiologists conducting workplace hearing conservation programs must calculate Time-Weighted Average (TWA) noise exposure and dose percentages for each employee based on varying noise levels throughout the shift. Manual calculation using OSHA's exchange rate formula is error-prone and time-consuming, especially for complex multi-exposure scenarios. Errors can lead to OSHA citations and missed hearing protection requirements.
who: Audiologists running occupational hearing conservation programs

skill_spec.name: OSHA Noise Exposure Calculator
skill_spec.one_liner: Calculates TWA, noise dose percentage, and required hearing protection based on employee exposure data per OSHA 29 CFR 1910.95.

inputs.name: exposures
inputs.label: List of noise levels (dBA) and durations (hours)

inputs.name: exchange_rate
inputs.label: Exchange rate (default 5 dB for OSHA, 3 dB for NIOSH)

outputs.name: action_required
outputs.label: Required action (hearing conservation program, protection, etc.)

outputs.name: max_exposure_time
outputs.label: Maximum allowable exposure time at given level

skill_spec.formula_hint: D = 100 * sum(C_i / T_i), where T_i = 8 / 2^((L_i - 90)/5) for OSHA. TWA = 16.61 * log10(D/100) + 90. Action level at 50% dose / 85 dBA TWA.

title: Hearing Aid Cost and Insurance Coverage Estimation
problem: Patients always ask about total out-of-pocket costs for hearing aids before committing to treatment. Audiologists must mentally juggle device costs, fitting fees, follow-up visits, insurance coverage limits, Medicare limitations, and state mandates for hearing aid coverage. Inaccurate estimates lead to patient frustration, abandoned fittings, and lost revenue.
who: Private practice and clinic audiologists counseling patients on hearing aid options

skill_spec.name: Hearing Aid Cost Estimator
skill_spec.one_liner: Estimates total patient cost for hearing aids including device, fitting, follow-ups, and insurance/benefit offsets.

inputs.name: insurance_type
inputs.label: Insurance type (Medicare, Medicaid, private, VA, none)

title: Hearing Aid Fitting Verification Checklist
problem: Hearing aid fitting involves 15+ verification steps including real-ear measurements, electroacoustic analysis, speech mapping, patient subjective feedback, and documentation. Skipping steps (especially real-ear measurement) leads to poor outcomes, patient returns, and potential liability. Studies show only 30-40% of audiologists consistently perform real-ear measurements despite being best practice.
who: All dispensing audiologists, especially newer clinicians

skill_spec.name: Hearing Aid Fitting Verification Protocol
skill_spec.one_liner: Complete step-by-step checklist for hearing aid fitting verification ensuring best-practice compliance including real-ear measurements.
steps: Step 1: Review audiogram and confirm hearing aid selection matches prescription (NAL-NL2 or DSL v5)
Step 2: Perform otoscopy - check for cerumen, canal conditions
Step 3: Verify hearing aid electroacoustic performance (ANSI S3.22 coupler measurements)
Step 4: Place probe tube in ear canal - mark at tragus + 28-30mm for adults
Step 5: Measure REUR (Real Ear Unaided Response)
Step 6: Insert hearing aid and measure REAR (Real Ear Aided Response) at 55, 65, 75 dB input
Step 7: Compare REAR to prescriptive targets - adjust gain if deviation >5 dB at key frequencies
Step 8: Run speech mapping with live speech or recorded passage
Step 9: Verify MPO (Maximum Power Output) with 85-90 dB sweep - must not exceed UCL
Step 10: Perform aided speech-in-noise testing (QuickSIN or HINT)
Step 11: Counsel patient on device use, insertion, cleaning, battery/charging
Step 12: Set up smartphone app and connectivity features
Step 13: Schedule follow-up appointments (1 week, 1 month, 3 months)
Step 14: Document all measurements and settings in patient record
Step 15: Confirm warranty registration and review return/trial period policy
warnings: Warning: Never skip real-ear measurement - subjective-only fitting leads to 10-15 dB prescription errors
Warning: Check MPO against UCL to prevent acoustic trauma
Warning: Document trial period start date - most states mandate 30-60 day return window

title: OSHA Hearing Conservation Program Compliance Checklist
problem: Audiologists managing workplace hearing conservation programs must ensure full compliance with OSHA 29 CFR 1910.95. The standard has 8 major components, each with specific requirements for noise monitoring, audiometric testing, hearing protection, training, and recordkeeping. Missing any element during an OSHA inspection leads to citations ranging from $16,131 to $161,323 per violation.
who: Industrial/occupational audiologists and audiologists consulting for employers

skill_spec.name: OSHA Hearing Conservation Compliance Checklist
skill_spec.one_liner: Complete compliance checklist for OSHA 29 CFR 1910.95 hearing conservation programs with all required elements and documentation.
steps: Step 1: Noise monitoring - Confirm area/personal noise surveys performed, identify all workers exposed ≥85 dBA TWA (action level)
Step 2: Audiometric testing program - Baseline audiogram within 6 months of first exposure (or 1 year if mobile van used with interim HPD), annual audiograms for all included employees
Step 3: Standard Threshold Shift (STS) evaluation - Compare annual to baseline, flag ≥10 dB average shift at 2000/3000/4000 Hz in either ear, age-correct per Appendix F if desired
Step 4: STS follow-up - Notify employee within 21 days of determination, refit/retrain HPD, refer for clinical evaluation if needed, record on OSHA 300 log if work-related and meets criteria
Step 5: Hearing protection - Make HPDs available at no cost to all workers ≥85 dBA TWA, mandatory use ≥90 dBA TWA or after STS, ensure NRR-based attenuation achieves <85 dBA exposure
Step 6: Training program - Annual training on: effects of noise, purpose of HPDs and audiometric testing, proper HPD use and care
Step 7: Recordkeeping - Maintain audiometric records for duration of employment, noise exposure records per 29 CFR 1910.95(m)
Step 8: Audiometer calibration - Daily biological check, annual acoustic calibration, exhaustive calibration every 2 years per ANSI S3.6
warnings: Warning: OSHA penalties up to $16,131/serious violation, $161,323/willful violation (2026 adjusted rates)
Warning: Baseline audiogram must be preceded by 14 hours of quiet (no workplace noise exposure or HPD use during quiet period)
Warning: Audiometric testing must be performed by licensed/certified audiologist, physician, or technician under their supervision
regulatory_refs: OSHA Penalty Adjustment per Federal Civil Penalties Inflation Adjustment Act

title: Standard Threshold Shift Calculation and OSHA Recordability
problem: After annual audiometric testing, audiologists must compare results to baselines to identify Standard Threshold Shifts (STS). The calculation requires averaging threshold changes at 2000, 3000, and 4000 Hz, optionally applying age correction factors from OSHA Appendix F, and determining OSHA 300 log recordability. Errors in STS determination lead to missed notifications (required within 21 days), incorrect OSHA logs, and potential citations.
who: Audiologists managing occupational hearing conservation programs

skill_spec.name: STS Calculator with OSHA Age Correction
skill_spec.one_liner: Calculates Standard Threshold Shift per OSHA 29 CFR 1910.95 with optional age correction (Appendix F) and determines recordability.

inputs.name: apply_age_correction
inputs.label: Apply OSHA Appendix F age correction?

outputs.name: avg_shift_raw
outputs.label: Average threshold shift (dB) without age correction

outputs.name: avg_shift_corrected
outputs.label: Average threshold shift (dB) with age correction

skill_spec.formula_hint: Shift at each freq = annual - baseline. Avg shift = (shift_2k + shift_3k + shift_4k) / 3. Age correction = Appendix F value at annual age minus Appendix F value at baseline age for each freq. STS = avg shift ≥ 10 dB. Recordable if STS + 25 dB average hearing level at 2k/3k/4k in same ear.

title: Newborn Hearing Screening Protocol and Follow-Up
problem: Audiologists conducting newborn hearing screenings must follow strict JCIH (Joint Committee on Infant Hearing) guidelines with specific timelines: screen by 1 month, diagnose by 3 months, intervene by 6 months (1-3-6 rule). Each step has required procedures, documentation, and follow-up actions. Missed follow-ups are the biggest gap in early hearing detection - nearly 50% of infants who fail screening are lost to follow-up.

skill_spec.name: Newborn Hearing Screening & Follow-Up Protocol
skill_spec.one_liner: Step-by-step protocol for newborn hearing screening, diagnostic follow-up, and early intervention referral per JCIH 2019 guidelines.
steps: Step 1: Initial screening - OAE and/or automated ABR before hospital discharge (by 1 month of age)
Step 2: Document results in medical record and state EHDI (Early Hearing Detection and Intervention) system
Step 3: PASS both ears - Provide parent education, document, schedule routine follow-up per risk factors
Step 4: REFER one or both ears - Schedule outpatient rescreen within 2 weeks, counsel parents (not a diagnosis)
Step 5: Outpatient rescreen - Repeat OAE/ABR in diagnostic setting
Step 6: If rescreen = REFER - Schedule comprehensive diagnostic ABR by 3 months of age
Step 7: Diagnostic ABR - Frequency-specific ABR, bone conduction ABR, tympanometry, determine type/degree/configuration
Step 8: Confirmed hearing loss - Refer to early intervention (Part C) within 2 days, audiology follow-up within 1 month
Step 9: Hearing aid fitting by 6 months of age (1 month after diagnosis if possible)
Step 10: Ongoing monitoring - Audiologic evaluation every 3 months for first year, every 6 months ages 1-3
Step 11: Risk factor monitoring - Children with CMV, NICU stay >5 days, family history: monitor even if passed initial screen
warnings: Warning: Lost-to-follow-up rate is ~45% nationally - implement tracking system and follow-up calls
Warning: NICU infants must receive ABR (not OAE alone) to detect auditory neuropathy spectrum disorder
Warning: State reporting to EHDI system is mandated - check state-specific requirements
regulatory_refs: State newborn hearing screening mandates (all 50 states + DC)
